interest: Shows 1931-37 US tracking of Japan's shift from open currency policy to controls prioritizing military rearmament.
overview: This file comprises the Department of State's official six-page List of Papers (docket sheets / purport list) for decimal file 894.5151, documenting Japanese foreign exchange policies, currency depreciation, and exchange control regulations from December 1931 through October 1937. Assembled under the subject heading 'Exchange - Japan', the entries record diplomatic despatches, telegrams, and economic memoranda from American officials—notably Ambassador Joseph C. Grew and Commercial Attaché Frank S. Williams in Tokyo, consular officers in Seoul, Beirut, and Shanghai, and State Department economic advisers Herbert Feis and Frederick Livesey—alongside interdepartmental correspondence with the U.S. Treasury Department and private inquiries from American financial firms. The papers trace the evolution of Japan's monetary policy following its departure from the gold standard, starting with initial rumors and laws to prevent capital flight in 1932, proceeding through the impacts of American monetary and silver-purchase policies, and culminating in the drastic exchange restrictions, import licensing regimes, and emergency control legislation (such as Law No. 87 of September 1937) enacted to support Japanese rearmament and military operations in China.

subfiles.about: A cumulative six-page docket list cataloguing State Department correspondence, telegrams, and cross-reference sheets concerning Japanese exchange control, currency depreciation, and capital flight from 1931 to 1937.
subfiles.summary: This sub-file consists of the complete, continuous six-page Department of State 'List of Papers' (Form DS-66 docket sheets) for decimal file 894.5151, summarizing records on Japanese foreign exchange policy between December 1931 and October 1937. It records despatches, telegrams, and memoranda from the American Embassy in Tokyo, consular posts in Seoul, Beirut, and Shanghai, and State Department economic advisers tracking the depreciation of the yen, gold export embargoes, and capital flight legislation. Later entries document the implementation of stringent import exchange licensing in 1937, the enactment of Law No. 87 by the Japanese Diet to prioritize military rearmament, and representations made regarding frozen American funds and blocked cotton futures balances.
